t: Rabbits in Forest — Greedy Grouping by Answer
o:
Each rabbit reports how many *other* rabbits share its color, so a color group containing a rabbit that answered $x$ has exactly $x+1$ rabbits total. Rabbits giving the same answer *may* share a color, but only if they fit in one group of size answer+1; otherwise they must belong to different groups. We want the minimum total rabbits consistent with all answers.

**Example 1** `[1,1,2]`: the two rabbits answering 1 can form one group of size 2 (no extra rabbits needed). The rabbit answering 2 needs a group of size 3, so 2 unseen rabbits join it. Total = 2 + 3 = 5.

**Example 2** `[10,10,10]`: each group of answer 10 holds 11 rabbits. Three rabbits fit in a single group of 11 (10 others + themselves), so we need 11 rabbits total — 8 of them never answered.

Constraints are tiny ($n \le 1000$, values < 1000), so any counting-based approach works easily; the challenge is purely the greedy grouping logic.
k: A rabbit answering x implies its color group has exactly x+1 members.
Count answers with a hash map: for count c of answer x, the number of groups needed is ceil(c / (x+1)), each contributing x+1 rabbits.
The greedy is optimal because packing same-answer rabbits into full groups minimizes the number of groups.

a.i: Simulate filling groups directly: keep a map from answer value to remaining capacity in the currently open group for that answer. When a rabbit answers x, if an open group has room, place it there; otherwise open a new group of size x+1 and add x+1 to the total. This mirrors the problem statement literally and is easy to reason about.
s: Maintain a map `open` mapping answer x to remaining slots in its current partially-filled group.
For each rabbit with answer x: if open[x] > 0, decrement it and continue.
Otherwise add x+1 to total and set open[x] = x (slots left in this new group).
a.t: O(n) — single pass over answers with O(1) map operations per element.
a.sp: O(n) — the map can hold up to n distinct answer keys.

a.i: Instead of simulating slot-by-slot, count occurrences of each answer. If answer x appears c times, those rabbits must be split into ceil(c / (x+1)) groups, each of size x+1, contributing ceil(c/(x+1)) * (x+1) rabbits. This closed-form avoids tracking partial groups and is the cleanest formulation.
s: Build a frequency map of all answers.
For each distinct answer x with frequency c, compute g = ceil(c / (x+1)) using integer math: (c + x) / (x + 1).
a.t: O(n) — one pass to count plus one pass over at most n distinct answers.
a.sp: O(n) — frequency map size bounded by number of distinct answers.

w: In an interview, go straight to the counting/ceiling-division solution after stating the key insight that answer x means a group of size x+1; mention the simulation variant briefly if asked to justify correctness greedily. **Pitfalls:** forgetting that answer counts *other* rabbits (group size is x+1, not x); using floor instead of ceiling division when c doesn't divide evenly into x+1; assuming rabbits with different answers can share a color (they cannot). **Edge cases:** answer 0 means a unique color (each such rabbit adds exactly 1); all-equal answers like [10,10,10]. **Follow-ups:** what's the maximum possible forest size (give every same-answer rabbit its own group: sum of c*(x+1)); how would you handle answers arriving as a stream (same algorithm works online).
